claims.text: Controlled annealing in an ammonia-rich atmosphere will introduce nitrogen into the multi-principal-element alloy catalyst.
The nitrogen-doping treatment will form multiple metal–nitrogen bonds.
The ammonia annealing treatment will produce a modest Pt-enriched surface layer.
Metal–nitrogen bonding stabilizes the alloy lattice.
Nitrogen incorporation adjusts adsorption energetics at active sites.
The adjusted adsorption energetics promote low-temperature CO and hydrocarbon oxidation.
Nitrogen incorporation repels or suppresses adsorption of H2O and NO poisoning species.
Nitrogen incorporation mitigates catalyst sintering during aging.
The combination of high entropy, multiple metal–nitrogen bonds, and a Pt-rich surface can improve catalyst durability.
The nitrogen-doped catalyst will have lower CO and hydrocarbon light-off temperatures than the untreated catalyst.
The nitrogen-doped catalyst will exhibit less deactivation in the presence of H2O and NO than the untreated catalyst.
The nitrogen-doped catalyst will show a slower performance decline under accelerated aging than the untreated catalyst.
The intervention can deliver the proposed benefits without adding platinum.
A high-entropy PtCoFeNiCu electrocatalyst architecture can provide lower platinum usage than conventional Pt electrocatalysts.
The benefits should apply during transient automotive exhaust operation below 150 °C in the presence of H2O and NO.
A uniform and sufficient density of metal–nitrogen bonds is required for the proposed improvements.
The proposed benefits will be less pronounced when nitrogen doping is incomplete or operating conditions exceed the anticipated range.
The optimal nitrogen-doping level and long-term stability of the metal–nitrogen bonds under real-world exhaust remain undetermined.
